action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with the iNPH markers and contrast
action_criteria.rationale: In a breast cancer survivor the MRI must both characterise the ventriculomegaly and look for leptomeningeal or parenchymal enhancement before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.rationale: Blood tests do not diagnose iNPH; here they screen for metabolic contributors, and the tumour marker adds little to the CSF and MRI.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 15 cmH2O, normal cells, protein and glucose; cytology without malignant cells, flow cytometry without an abnormal population; 40 mL removed; TUG 27 to 19 s at 24 hours (30%), 10-metre walk 21 to 14 s, MoCA 22 to 25
action_criteria.label: Lumbar tap test with opening pressure and CSF cytology
action_criteria.rationale: The same puncture must measure the opening pressure and the gait response and send cytology, because leptomeningeal carcinomatosis is the alternative the oncology team raised.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 21 s at 2 hours and 19 s at 24 hours (30%), 10-metre walk 14 s (33%), MoCA 25/30, no incontinence
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the timed measures at 2 and 24 hours after the 40 mL tap gives her gait response, the evidence for a shunt once cytology has excluded carcinomatosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Flags the duloxetine-tamoxifen CYP2D6 problem and a venlafaxine alternative
action_criteria.label: Medication interaction review
action_criteria.rationale: Her antidepressant and her tamoxifen share a CYP2D6 pathway that matters for her cancer care, though not for the hydrocephalus decision.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not commit to iNPH without ruling out leptomeningeal disease by CSF cytology and contrast MRI in a patient with a history of breast cancer
Do not attribute the syndrome to cancer recurrence without CSF or imaging evidence of it
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 30% in TUG at 24 hours, the supportive MRI (tight high-convexity sulci, acute callosal angle) and normal-pressure CSF with negative cytology [Nakajima_2021]
Inform the oncologist that CSF cytology and flow cytometry are negative and contrast MRI shows no leptomeningeal or parenchymal disease, and continue tamoxifen with routine oncology surveillance

Review duloxetine with the oncologist: as a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor it may lower endoxifen levels and tamoxifen efficacy, so an antidepressant with minimal CYP2D6 inhibition (for example venlafaxine) is preferred [CPIC_tamoxifen_2018]
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a chronic gait and cognitive syndrome without seizures or fluctuating awareness
There is no syncope, palpitation or cardiac question in this gait and cognitive work-up
Echocardiography answers no question in this work-up: there is no cardioembolic event or heart failure
Head CT adds nothing once brain MRI is available, which measures the ventricles, callosal angle and DESH better
Rhythm monitoring has no role without syncope or a suspected arrhythmia
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Prion, inflammatory and infectious CSF assays answer no question in a chronic afebrile gait syndrome with normal CSF cells

differential.diagnosis: Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis or CNS metastasis from breast cancer
differential.key_features: Raised by the cancer history, but cytology and flow cytometry are negative, CSF cells and glucose are normal, there are no cranial nerve signs and contrast MRI shows no leptomeningeal or parenchymal enhancement.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Deep white matter disease is only Fazekas grade 1 without lacunes.
No rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia; the lower-body gait disorder improved after CSF removal.
Hippocampi are preserved (MTA 1) and recall improves with cueing, an executive rather than amnestic profile.
Tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle of 81 degrees argue against atrophy.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary communicating hydrocephalus (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic)
differential.key_features: No head injury, haemorrhage, meningitis or cranial irradiation precedes the decline.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires insidious onset after age 40, at least 3 to 6 months of progression, no antecedent such as trauma, haemorrhage or meningitis, and a gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms [Relkin_2005]
Imaging: Evans index 0.35 without obstruction, with tight high-convexity sulci, a callosal angle of 81 degrees and temporal horn enlargement [Nakajima_2021]

Normal opening pressure (15 cmH2O) with normal CSF content; TUG improved 30% at 24 hours after a 40 mL tap, above the 10% TUG improvement commonly used as a positive threshold (no guideline sets a single cut-off)
Tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% with PPV 73% to 100% [Marmarou_2005]

In a cancer survivor, negative CSF cytology on the tap sample with no leptomeningeal enhancement on contrast MRI makes leptomeningeal carcinomatosis unlikely; a single negative cytology does not exclude it absolutely, so new cranial nerve or radicular signs would justify repeat sampling

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Negative cytology and flow cytometry, normal CSF cells and glucose and no enhancement on contrast MRI make leptomeningeal disease unlikely, and the magnetic gait with a tap response indicates iNPH.
red_herrings.data_point: Breast cancer (lumpectomy, radiation and chemotherapy 6 years ago, in clinical remission on tamoxifen)
red_herrings.intended_effect: The syndrome is presumptively attributed to leptomeningeal carcinomatosis and NPH is not pursued

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

interactions: Duloxetine with tamoxifen: duloxetine is a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor and may reduce conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite endoxifen, potentially lowering its efficacy. Avoid the combination where possible; antidepressants with minimal CYP2D6 inhibition (for example venlafaxine) are preferred.
Amlodipine: no clinically relevant interaction with tamoxifen or duloxetine.

patient.history_present_illness: A 69-year-old retired nurse with breast cancer in clinical remission (6 years post-treatment) was admitted for urgent neurological evaluation of progressive gait deterioration, memory decline, and urinary incontinence over the past 10 months. She was treated with lumpectomy, radiation, and chemotherapy (doxorubicin-cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel) 6 years ago and has been in clinical remission on tamoxifen maintenance. Her oncology team is concerned that the gait deterioration, cognitive decline and urinary incontinence could represent leptomeningeal carcinomatosis or CNS metastasis, and requested urgent neurology consultation. She describes progressive shuffling gait beginning 10 months ago, three falls (no injury), and increasing reliance on a walker. Urinary urgency began approximately 7 months ago, progressing to frank incontinence 2-3 times per week. She describes increasing forgetfulness and difficulty following complex nursing reports she used to review voluntarily. Her oncologist noticed the gait change at a routine visit. A neurology fellow who examined her noted that the gait had a distinctly magnetic quality.

neurological_exam.additional: No meningismus. No papilledema. No cranial nerve palsies. Bilateral grasp reflexes present. No skin lesions suggesting metastases.

neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, shuffling magnetic gait with freezing on initiation; uses a walker. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test: 2 steps backward. Timed gait measures reported separately.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3. Anxious about cancer recurrence. Slowed responses, normal language, no aphasia. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone and strength. No focal deficits. No radiculopathic signs.
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal throughout. No dermatomal sensory loss.
